components.text: The decisive comparative demand fails if the cited evidence is equally expected under non-God alternatives.
The emergent-spacetime evidence must discriminate a mind from nonmental alternatives.
The decisive demand is whether theism has a discriminator making it more probable than alternatives that accommodate the same evidence.
The mindlike-structure argument must show why shared informational features favor mind over nonmental emergence.
The consciousness argument must distinguish a personal God from non-theistic fundamental-consciousness alternatives.
The claimed personal and divine properties of the foundational consciousness require an available form of justification.
A comparative conclusion needs warrant for the extra properties attributed to the preferred explanation.
The decisive demand is whether evidence warrants identifying a necessary ground as a personal mind or God.
The comparative conclusion requires warranted divine properties rather than freely assigned metaphysical predicates.
Theism's claimed parsimony must account for the explanatory cost of its additional divine properties.
Identifying a personal source as God introduces properties requiring independent explanatory work.
The decisive demand is whether theism's additional divine properties earn their cost in the claimed parsimony comparison.
Calling the personal fundamental source God requires properties not shared by thinner alternatives.
A simpler account is not preferable unless it adequately explains all relevant data.
Equal accommodation requires explanatory adequacy rather than mere logical compatibility.
The decisive demand is whether a simpler alternative remains preferable if it fails to explain relevant data.
Emergent spacetime must favor a mind over viable emergence from nonmental natural properties.
The decisive demand is whether emergent spacetime positively discriminates a cosmic mind from natural foundational properties.
The natural alternative must remain scientifically viable rather than win merely through abstract simplicity.
The proper demand is comparative best-explanation warrant, not proof or absolute certainty about metaphysical reality.
Comparative counterarguments can assess metaphysical explanations without claiming deductive proof.
The decisive demand is reframed from absolute proof to comparative, defeasible inference to the best explanation.
Comparative abduction must still identify why theism explains better rather than merely being possible.
Current failure to explain consciousness does not establish a new fundamental mental ontology.
Rejected or minority quantum-consciousness interpretations do not independently establish cosmic mind.
The decisive demand is whether unexplained consciousness warrants fundamental mind rather than an undiscovered physical basis.
The digital-physics and observer arguments must establish mentality rather than mere compatibility.
A comparative abduction requires a warranted simplicity comparison between physical and new ontological explanations.
The inference to fundamental consciousness must overcome induction from prior successful natural explanations.
The decisive demand is whether explanatory history supports expecting a natural cause of consciousness instead of fundamental mind.
The abductive comparison must incorporate the claimed inductive base rate for natural explanations.
Deeper natural laws do not exclude mind-first explanation if their foundational properties are genuinely mindlike.
The decisive demand is whether deeper natural laws exclude or actually rival a mind-first account.
Calling deeper properties natural does not by itself show that they are nonmental or explanatorily preferable.
The shared need for a necessary foundation answers the regress question but leaves its identity contested.
Theism and naturalistic pantheism offer competing identifications of the same necessary role.
The decisive demand is what terminates contingent dependence and whether the resulting necessary foundation may be identified as God.
The known universe's beginning and dependence are offered against treating it as the final foundation.
A cosmic natural foundation could occupy the same regress-ending role assigned to God.
The decisive demand is whether only God can occupy the regress-ending role or whether an infinite natural cosmos can do so.
A nonmental cosmic foundation remains an alternative to the claimed governing mind.
A foundation built from reducible natural parts would continue dependence rather than terminate it.
An undiscovered physical basis composed of parts would require further explanation.
The decisive demand is whether a reducible natural conscious cause could terminate rather than continue explanatory dependence.
The move must justify consciousness as the stopping point rather than merely declaring it fundamental.
Incomplete direct data does not prevent constructing and comparing coherent metaphysical explanatory models.
Idealism, theism, and natural alternatives can be compared as models despite limited access to ultimate foundations.
The decisive demand is whether incomplete direct access precludes building warranted metaphysical explanatory models.
Competing metaphysical models still require comparative evidential discrimination.
The analogy with physical theory fails if God is not composed from physical principles, particles, or laws.
A cosmic mind is not thereby a physical explanation of emergent spacetime.
The decisive demand is whether invoking God or consciousness qualifies as a physical theory comparable to theoretical physics.
Mindlike foundational properties would need representation in physical principles, particles, or laws.
A bounded claim about justifiable human knowledge is not an unrestricted metaphysical claim and is therefore not self-refuting.
The decisive challenge is whether limiting justified human knowledge is itself an unrestricted, self-refuting metaphysical claim.
Defeasible metaphysical inference remains possible within a human-knowledge limitation.
Brain-consciousness correlation does not by itself establish neural production of subjective experience.
An idealist interface model offers a nonproductive interpretation of the same neural correlations.
The decisive demand is whether neural correlations establish production of subjective experience rather than merely systematic association.
The brain-interface model supplies an idealist accommodation of the same neural evidence.
The move does not challenge the limited scope of the con epistemic claim.
